question: A 19-year-old sustains a nasal injury in a fight. Examination shows boggy, bilateral, fluctuant swelling of the nasal septum that is non-tender and obliterates both nasal passages. The most appropriate immediate management is:

answers.text: Prescribe a course of oral antibiotics and review in 48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Antibiotics alone will not drain the haematoma. Delay risks avascular necrosis of the septal cartilage within 3-4 days, leading to a permanent saddle nose deformity.

answers.text: Pack both nasal cavities with ribbon gauze to compress the swelling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Nasal packing would compress but not drain the haematoma, and would not prevent cartilage necrosis. Drainage with incision is required.

answers.text: Incise and drain the haematoma under local anaesthesia and apply a through-and-through suture or quilting to prevent reaccumulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Septal haematoma must be drained urgently. Incision and drainage, followed by quilting sutures or a firm nasal dressing to obliterate the dead space, prevents reaccumulation. This is the most preventable catastrophe in ENT trauma.

answers.text: Arrange elective CT paranasal sinuses and refer to the next available ENT outpatient clinic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. This is an emergency requiring same-day drainage. Delay of even 48-72 hours can result in cartilage necrosis and permanent cosmetic deformity or functional obstruction.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the management of septal haematoma. Delay allows avascular necrosis of the septal cartilage, as the cartilage derives its nutrition solely from the overlying perichondrium.
Well done. Septal haematoma is the most preventable catastrophe in nasal trauma. Immediate incision and drainage with dead-space obliteration is mandatory.
